title: Compassion For Charleston
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching is that true freedom and peace can be found by embracing the present moment, even in the midst of suffering and uncertainty. This requires cultivating patience, compassion, and understanding, not just for ourselves, but also for others who may be struggling with pain and hatred. By acknowledging our own limitations and vulnerabilities, we can begin to see the interconnectedness of all beings and find ways to heal and transform suffering, rather than simply trying to transcend or escape it.
topics: the Buddha's verse on various roles and identities

sentences.text: Well, I was planning to speak a little bit about time, the timeless quality it seems like we experience each year when we come back here.
And maybe you know what I mean, whether you've been here 20 years in a row or for the first time.
There's some felt experience of being here as if we never left.
It doesn't exactly feel like we were doing something else for 51 weeks and now we're back again for week number 52.
It doesn't really feel that way.
It feels more like we've always been here: some sense of connection with something beyond our usual idea of time.
Sometimes this feeling, whatever this feeling is, seems to manifest also as a sense of place, a sense of location and space.
So sometimes we think about the sky here and the water and the birds and the history of this spot.
Or maybe it's something about seasonal time, that we come here each year at the exact same season, just before and during and after the solstice.
Somehow we've had the good fortune to be here pretty much every year, I think, maybe except one or two, over the solstice.

We sit through the longest day of the year and somehow in our bodies feel the shifting of the path of the sun, from its widest arc from the northeast around to the northwest, like it almost gets back to where it started again.
Then while we're sitting here it starts to narrow back down towards east to west, and eventually, after the equinox, southeast to southwest.
So maybe this sense of timelessness and boundlessness has to do with that.
We're in summer feeling the very beginning of winter, the turning.
So somehow we're here through all the seasons.
So we don't even know really: is this a week of sitting or a year of sitting?
And at first, when we were starting our sangha, and many of you here have been involved in the startings of sanghas, it actually just felt like a neat discovery.
Wow, it's really more convenient and easier to organize events if you do the same thing at the same time every year.
You can get out the same file, you don't have to change as much.
Of course it was paper files at first, and now those are all lost and it's computer files.
This sense of consistency year after year just seemed like a great idea, very convenient, made it easier.
And Norman's journeys, and he's journeying at the moment actually, he's probably just gotten on the plane in San Francisco, have added to the sense of seasonality and irregularity and timelessness.
Perhaps Norman coming here to the Bellingham area and to the Vancouver area at the exact same time every year, year after year, like a migrating bird or something like that.
But maybe it's more than just practical.
Maybe we actually sort of stumbled into something that humans have done since the beginning: seasonal celebrations, a festival year.
Sometimes there are stories behind the seasonal celebrations of groups of humans.
Maybe the stories came first or maybe the celebration came first, I don't know.
Celebrations from religious stories, celebrations from seasonal stories.
So maybe this isn't just a convenience, to come at the same time every year, but a sort of returning to something deeply and necessarily human.
Maybe it's sort of like gates into a sacred sense of time.
So I was planning to speak about all this, and I think it's interesting and fun to talk about and think about and feel into, because we don't usually have a lot of time for this kind of thing, right?
We're too busy.
And I stumbled across a book by a religious scholar.
I'm far from a scholar, but I stumble into stuff.
A religious scholar named, I think it's pronounced, Mircea Iliade.
He has a well-known book, I guess.
I guess it's well-known.
I heard about it.
It's called The Sacred and the Profane, published in the 50s.
Some reference to what I saw.
And he was really interested in this topic.
Here's a little paragraph from Professor Iliade.
*For religious people, time, just like space, is neither homogenous nor continuous.
On the one hand, there are intervals of a sacred time.
The time of festivals, by far the greater part of which are periodical.
And on the other hand, there is profane time, ordinary temporal duration in which acts without religious meaning have their setting.
Between these two kinds of time, sacred and profane, there is of course solution of continuity.
By means of rites, religious people can pass through without danger,* he says,
*without danger from ordinary temporal duration to sacred time.* That's nice, huh?
Maybe a little more dualistic than Dogen, but a powerful thought, that we need rites and rituals and seasonal celebrations as a passage, as a passageway back to sacred time.
So anyway, I started preparing this talk on Monday or Tuesday morning, and then I was going to finish it up yesterday morning.
I finished writing it.
And then on Wednesday, a young man entered a church.
I didn't know any of this at the time, but I've read up a little bit.
A young man entered a deeply historic black church in Charleston, South Carolina.
The church is called Emmanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church.
I understand it's usually called Emmanuel or Emmanuel A.M.E. or Mother Emmanuel, Mother Emmanuel.
I don't know if they would say "I'm going to Mother," but maybe they do.
The church was founded in 1816, 200 years ago next year, and somehow it was founded by people who were at the time enslaved.
I don't know how that happens, but somehow they could do it.
It took me a minute or a while for this to sink in.
For many Americans, if you say something historic happened 200 years ago, to me that just sounds like, oh, that's cool.
That's very historic.
Historic is a good quality.
It has a certain weight and solidness to it.
Maybe kind of dimly in the past, but historic.
It rings with some goodness.
But then I realized that for quite a few of my countrypeople, if you're talking about something 200 years ago, it means you're talking about your family, your ancestors, enslaved.
Really, so many things are like that.
I don't think about it, but they are, right?

You could talk to a Jewish person about 80 years ago, or a Rwandan person about 30 years ago, a Cambodian person about however long that was, 35, 40 years ago, or maybe a Mexican person about last year.
And maybe that history is a pretty difficult history of atrocity and pain, narrowness and division.
A historic place could be historic because it rings with horror.
And it could also be a place echoing with redemption and change.
So one of the founders of Emmanuel A.M.E., I learned, himself a slave, was to be a leader in a slave rebellion.
He was one of the organizers of an attempt to end slavery from the inside.
In 1822, six years after Emmanuel was founded, this rebellion was crushed brutally, as I think they all were. 35 people are known to have been killed, probably more.
And the rebellion being associated with the church, they burned the church down, burned it to the ground.
And somehow they rebuilt this church.
It makes me really curious to talk to a historian.
How was it even possible in that situation to rebuild your church?
I don't think you just went to Home Depot to get supplies and started building.
How did they do it?

I don't know, but they rebuilt it, continued or restarted worship in the church, and then the city of Charleston shut down all churches and all religious meetings by African-American people, black people, in 1835.
So then they met in secret for 30 years, it said there.
That's amazing to me, that a sentence in a book, or a Wikipedia page in this case, one sentence could say that: and then they met in secret for 30 years.
What does that actually mean?

I have to admit to a little bit of pride arising at times that we have been having this retreat here on Sandwich Island every year, for we're not sure exactly how many years, a little proud of the fact that we can't remember exactly, but 20 years, 21 years.
But it's probably a lot easier for us than worshiping in secret in Charleston, South Carolina, as an enslaved person in the 1830s, 40s, and 50s.
Then in 1865, which I think would be immediately after the collapse of the Confederacy, the church was reopened.
It had boards over the windows or what, but the church was reopened.
And amazingly it was reorganized, and the leader of the reopening was the son of the original founder who organized that slave rebellion, 43 years later.
This life under oppression, risking their lives in practice, 30 years in secret, reopening the church.
The year after that was Juneteenth.
Do you know about Juneteenth?
I learned about this too.
The next year in Texas, on June the 19th, the Union General, who was the occupying governor, gave a big speech and let everybody know that they were free.
The white slave owners had managed to keep the Emancipation Proclamation secret and hidden for nearly two years.
So Juneteenth is a holiday in Texas to this day.
So it was about that time.
So it was no accident, apparently, that a young white man named Dylan Roof picked this place on Wednesday night.
He entered the church at about 8 o'clock in the evening, joining a Bible study group, presumably scheduled and on the website of the sign.
There were 12 people at the meeting, all long-term members of the church.
At first he listened and seemed to be participating with everyone.
Then he started arguing points of scripture and getting, I guess, kind of belligerent.
And then he got up and pulled out a gun.
He'd been there about an hour.
One of the men present there, I'll tell you his name, Twanza Sanders, who was 26, tried to talk him down.
"Why are you doing this?
Why do you want to make violence in the church?"
And one of the witnesses remembers Dylan Roof, and we're assuming it's Dylan Roof.
I mean, the justice system has not operated, but it seems likely, maybe it could possibly be somebody else.
But someone who was probably him was remembered to have said, "I have to do it.
You rape our woman.
You're taking over our country.
And you have to go."
And he explained that he was planning to shoot everybody.
Two people survived by playing dead.
One person survived the gunshot wound.
And one person he deliberately spared, explaining that he wanted somebody to be able to tell what had happened, what he had done.
I have no way of understanding why something like this could happen.
A representative of the Southern Poverty Law Center, who keeps tabs on hate groups in the South, made a few points.
She said that membership in these groups is growing steadily and that the Internet has greatly facilitated their growth.

In the same way the Internet can allow people to connect along all sorts of very specialized personal interests and create things like online Buddhist courses and Etsy, there's some specialized group for just about anything.
It's amazing, really, right?
The Internet has facilitated so many amazing things: people in isolated, disparate places connecting and helping each other in a way that never could have happened before.
So the Internet's keeping a lot of things alive, and a lot of specialized skills and knowledge and person-to-person connections have been facilitated, as has hatred, as has racism.
And she said another focus of these groups is a demographic projection.
The demographic projection is that by some time in the middle of the century, non-Caucasian people will probably outnumber Caucasian people in America.
So that's a focus of their rhetoric and, I guess, what they think about members of these groups.
And the idea of rape of a white woman, she reminded us, is as old as the beginnings of racism and slavery.
And here those words are on the lips of a 21-year-old man with a gun in 2015.

The victims were Cynthia Marie Graham Hurd, 54; Susie Jackson, 87; Ethel Lee Lance, 70; DePayne Middleton, 49; Clementa Pinkney, 41, who is also the pastor and is also a state senator of South Carolina, and also somebody who has been actively involved in police brutality cases and is interested in gun control.
And other victims: Tuanza Sanders, who tried to speak to the shooter, 26; Daniel Simmons, 74; Sharonda Coleman Singleton, 45; Myra Thompson, 59.
A few of the names remind me of a difficult conversation my wife and I had with a relative.
This relative is a football fan, really likes football.
Like most sports, they write the names on the backs of the jerseys and they say the names, sportscasting.
And as a fan, you want to know who's who and what's what and what's going on.
This relative was complaining about these names, like Tuanza and DePayne, that they're not ordinary names and they're hard to hear and hard to understand, and in fact she has hearing loss.
So it was powerfully interesting to have had that conversation a couple of days, that's like the day before I think this happened.
We were hearing this from our relative.

Janet was trying to remind her, her understanding being that it's a value in African American society and black American society to have a unique name, and that there are many hundreds of thousands of unique new names picked every year.
Here are these people with these unique names being killed.

The next day, very quickly, I don't know why it happened so quickly, the suspected shooter Dylan Roof, I don't know if it was an arraignment or a pre-arraignment, I don't know all the legal details, but he was interviewed.
He was in the jail somewhere and they had him on a video screen, and he was briefly interviewed by one of the justice officials, his name and who he was and whether he was employed.
For some reason it was very important for the justice official to find out if he was employed.
He asked him several times to clarify that he was unemployed.
And then in another room they had relatives of the victims and they were able to communicate over a video link with Dylan Roof.
The shooting was on Wednesday night, and video of this was available online yesterday.
That's remarkable.
What the relatives of the victims chose to say to Dylan Roof was, "I forgive you."
I guess five people spoke, and you could hear three of them on the video, each one in a different way saying, "You have done a terrible thing.
This can hurt me more than anything in the world, to lose my son, my mom, and I forgive you."
Somehow, because of the practice of these people and the situation in this church for 200 years, a day or two after something like this there could be forgiveness.
This made me think of a poem I've read a couple of times lately by Naomi Shihab Nye called "Shoulders."
*A man crosses the street in rain, stepping gently, looking two times north and south because his son is asleep on his shoulder.
No car must splash him.
No car drive too near his shadow.
This man carries the world's most sensitive cargo, but he's not marked.
Nowhere does his jacket say fragile, handle with care.
His ears fill up with breathing.
He hears the hum of a boy's dream deep inside.
We're not going to be able to live in this world if we're not willing to do what he is doing with one another.
The road will only be wide.
The rain will never stop falling.*
*A man crosses the street in rain, stepping gently, looking two times north and south because his son is asleep on his shoulder.
No car must splash him.
No car drive too near to his shadow.
This man carries the world's most sensitive cargo, but he's not marked.
Nowhere does his jacket say fragile, handle with care.
His ear fills up with breathing.
He hears the hum of a boy's dream deep inside him.
We're not going to be able to live in this world if we're not willing to do what he is doing with one another.
The road will only be wide.
The rain will never stop falling.*
So I heard something had happened in South Carolina on Wednesday night after I got home from Zazen.

I'm trying to work on this bad habit I have of flicking the computer on, but I indulge nonetheless, and I looked at Facebook, I think, and the top posting was, "My heart goes out to the people of South Carolina."
It didn't say what had happened, so I got curious and I looked.
I briefly read the beginning of the article, and then I turned it off again and went to bed and forgot about it.
And Thursday was very busy, a lot of things to do.
I'm sure for many of you, you remember Thursday still, a long time ago.
Very busy day, getting ready to be here.
A lot of tasks, I had several meetings, and I didn't think about this.
And Thursday night, right, we're about to turn the lights out, about 10:30, 11, and a permanent issue with Janet and me is she always wants to go to bed just a little bit later than me.
So I've worked on my patience and compassion, but I have to admit I'm always slightly like, "Ah, let's go to bed already."

At that moment, her hand reaching for the switch, she says, "You know, the creepiest thing about that thing that happened in South Carolina is that he spent half an hour there, turns out maybe it was an hour, with them."
And I didn't want to hear about it.
I actually deflected it actively.
I said, "You know what, it's bedtime.
That's too creepy.
I don't want to hear about that."
And she was very patient with me, and said, "Okay," and the lights went out.
I went to bed.
Last Friday morning, I managed to finish writing the talk, and then it dawned on me that I really like wisdom.
Isn't wisdom nice?
The emptiness teachings, this tremendous gift of support that we've received in this tradition, to be stable, to be upright, to be able to let things go, to just be, and here we are, another week.
We don't have to do anything, really.
We just have to be.
And I realize that I really like this.
It's just so deeply comforting.
It makes me feel strong and safe, not without some pain and confusion.
Not only is this week at Samish timeless, it's also a certain kind of coming home for me and maybe for many of us here.
We're home together again with our siblings and our aunties and our uncles and our kids here.
We've all grown up together a lot here and come together little by little with the support of wisdom to feel, I think, a little fuller, a little more grounded, maybe a lot more grounded.
And Zen emphasizes wisdom, that there's nothing to hold onto, nothing to fear.
In the end, it's just fear.
That's all it is.
We can be with it.
We can be with anything.
But maybe wisdom just in itself isn't quite enough, isn't complete.
And this wisdom is, of course, imbued with and supportive of compassion.
They say that wisdom and compassion are like two wings of the bird of the practice of Buddhism.
I've never actually seen a citation for that, so the scholarly piece of me is like, "Where did that come from anyway?"
But it certainly seems true.
So I wanted to give a talk on wisdom, and I realized we have to talk about compassion.
We have to talk about both.
They're not separate.
They're not different.

When I trained a little bit at Stanford University on how to bring compassion training into the secular world, like the mindfulness work, one of the things that was interesting was that they suggested compassion is not just a state or an emotion or a personality quality, like, "Oh, he's so compassionate and she's not too compassionate," but a process.
Compassion is actually a process, which makes sense.
Nothing is fixed, right?
We know this from wisdom.
Everything is a process.
There's nothing that's not a process, even process is a process.
There's no thing there.
The first step in the process is actually noticing that there is suffering.
So I noticed that this thing had happened, at first.
But if we don't actually notice that there is suffering in our heart, in our mind, in the others around us, in this burning world, already we're off the trail.
Compassion won't result.
Now try again.
So let's say we notice that there was suffering.
And again, I think the stability of the wisdom practices may make us more available to suffering.
Conversely, it could make us able to block it out in our stability.
We can misuse just about anything, somehow.
The second step in the Stanford compassion program process is to actually feel something.
It's empathy.
It's empathy: to actually feel something directly in ourselves.
The noticing is kind of a perception, kind of cognitive: "Oh, something happened."
The second step, feeling, is more in our heart, in our gut.
So little by little, starting to feel something.
But this thing that happened, I only know through video and words, being so far away.
So we can certainly easily not feel something.
Maybe we can't help but feel something.
And once we've felt something, and of course, yeah, you can notice and not feel.
That's easy to do.
We have training in that.
Next is to be willing.
Next is to be willing.
To be willing to do something.
To be something.
To experience something.
To be present, too.
To be willing to hold the boy on our shoulder, and to be able to hear the hum of his dream.
That's a kind of willingness.
Maybe to be willing not to give a comfortable, and very clever, it was a really clever talk.
I'm sorry I can't give it.
Had nice koan references and poetry, the whole deal.
I've been listening to Norman do this for 30 years.
Not bad.
So, a willingness.
And one of the things that's interesting about compassion in the Buddhist frame is that when we think about actions, we think about body actions: we've got to go do something.
But actions of speech and actions of mind are also powerful.
They have a powerful karmic effect, have a powerful result, though somehow we might not know what the result is.
So I have no idea what to do about racism in the South.
I've never even been to the South.
I've never had the opportunity to attend a church like that.

And although it's spectacularly great that Western Zen has made some little progress, I think, with sexism, I don't know if they're more or less, we have maybe half and half genders or maybe a few more women here, it's good.
But we're kind of a white crowd, have you noticed?
So I don't know what to do.
And I know people in Brooklyn are thinking about this in a wiser way and are in a socioeconomic situation where it's maybe more logistically possible to experiment and learn.
But I can do my best.
We can all do our best to be willing to feel, willing to do what we can.
I saw also on Facebook that our colleague Florence Caplow, who is now a Unitarian Universalist minister, did you know that?
She's graduated in everything and has her first job.
She'll be the minister of a small congregation in Carbondale, Colorado, somewhere high up in the mountains.
And she's really effective with social media, too.
She does these brilliant little things with the right kind of picture.
Anyway, very nice, very good.
Well, man, wholesome.
Anyway, she said she went to a Baptist church in Port Townsend and they wrote cards and sent donations to Emmanuel Church in Charleston.
So we could certainly do that.
Nothing's stopping us.
Another thing we have at our fingertips is the power of vow and the power of dedication of merit.
Is it real?
Who knows?
What is real, anyway?
But maybe one thing that we are uniquely able to do, a beautiful contribution, is to dedicate the merit of this sesshin, the merit of our practice this week, to the suffering.
How you conceptualize that suffering: is it the suffering of the black community in the South?
Is it racism?
Is it slavery?
Is it greed, hate and delusion, writ large in so many fucking ways?
To me, we can dedicate our practice, whatever goodness comes from the sesshin, to the healing of suffering.
And be willing to suffer ourselves.
Not hide out in wisdom.
Let wisdom support us in stepping through that gate, not just into sacred time and sacred space, but sacred compassion, sacred love, sacred humanity.

One of the things I was looking forward to quoting, which is still germane, so I'll quote it nonetheless, is from when Dogen was thinking about time and space and he wrote his famous essay "Uji," "Being Time," or "The Time Being," [unclear: "Flavor and Feeling"] for which Ruth cleverly folded into a novel and used the publishing industry worldwide to broadcast.
It was really clever.
Good work.

He opened with a little quotation, a little poem, which he attributed to a Chinese Zen worthy, but I read the scholarly footnotes, and it turns out that's spurious, and he just pretty much cobbled it together from various sources.
He made it up.

So the opening verse of this essay he wrote about time and being, and how can we be in time, this time that is full of joy and light and connection, this time that is full of racism and violence, this time that's full of all time.
How can we be in this time?
And so I made my own little version of his verse, which is itself a translation.
Who knows?
Anyway.
*An old Buddha said, In being time, we stand on the highest peak.
In being time, we float in the deepest ocean.
In being time, we are demons and monsters.
In being time, we are Buddhas.
In being time, we are staffs and whisks.
In being time, we are lamps and cabins.
In being time, we are Harry and Sally and Tishon and Jolie.
In being time, we are the great earth.
We are the heavens.
We are everything.*
So maybe we can practice with this dance.
Time, space, compassion, wisdom, being demons.
We are, right?
We are.
We are the demons.
And being Buddhas, which we also are.
Being ordinary human beings.
Being heavens.
Being the whole world.

With the privilege that we enjoy this week of opening to sacred time, we can emerge next Saturday, if there is a next Saturday, not exactly purified, maybe clarified, so that we are a little more ready to help in a way that truly helps.
So thank you very much for listening to my talk.
I didn't really know it was going to happen.
On behalf of people who look like me, I'm really sorry about what happened there and all the other horrible things that have happened.
And we've spent a good time in the past year on the horrible things that happened here, in this place.
May the rivers and roads not be wide.
May the sun come out for all beings.
